passage:
Monday, 7:40 pm. Reena had meant to message alumni for three weeks. Every evening she argued with herself: too tired, too early, too awkward. She wrote a rule on a card: When the clock hits eight on a work night, two alumni get a message before supper.
Tuesday, eight o'clock. The alarm buzzed. She felt the usual pull to put it off, but the rule had already decided. She opened her list: two names, two short messages, sent in twelve minutes.
Thursday of the next week. Santosh, a senior at a mid-sized firm, replied: “Happy to chat on Saturday.” By then, sending had stopped feeling like a choice. It was simply what happened at eight.

qa.a: Santosh, a senior at a mid-sized firm, replied.

qa.q: How does Reena feel when the alarm buzzes on Tuesday?
qa.a: Reena feels the usual pull to put it off, but the rule has already decided, so she starts anyway.

qa.q: What could Reena do if a work night is impossible?
qa.a: Reena could set a backup time, such as a weekend morning, keeping the same if-then form so nothing is left to argue about.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel getting the message?
qa.a: Santosh is probably glad to be asked and happy to help, since the reply offers a chat on Saturday.

grounding: The student writes an if-then rule to send two messages to alumni at a fixed time, which removes the daily debate about whether to start.

passage: You're struggling to reach out to people, Sudha? Let me tell you how I got my first job, twenty years ago. I was twenty-one, in final year, and I hated asking anyone for anything. Every evening I'd sit down meaning to write to our alumni, and every evening I'd argue myself out of it: too tired, too awkward, tomorrow. My roommate Nirmala finally said, "Rekha, stop deciding every day. Decide once." So I wrote on a card above my desk: "Weekday, eight o'clock: two alumni messages, then I eat." That was all. No debate. At eight, I wrote two emails, even short ones, and then I ate. In six weeks I had sent about sixty. Five people replied. One of them, a senior named Mr. Pillai, got me an interview. Deciding once, Sudha, saved me from deciding a hundred times.

qa.q: What did the card above Rekha's desk say?
qa.a: Weekday, eight o'clock: two alumni messages, then I eat.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel about reaching out before the rule?
qa.a: Rekha felt awkward and reluctant, hating to ask anyone for anything and finding excuses every evening.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Choosing, after Nirmala's push, to decide once with an if-then rule, so eight o'clock meant writing without any debate.

qa.q: How did Nirmala see Rekha's evenings?
qa.a: Nirmala saw Rekha wasting energy re-deciding every day and pushed Rekha to decide once instead.

grounding: Shows a final-year student using an if-then rule, two alumni messages at 8 pm on weekdays, to end the daily debate about starting outreach.

passage: Sachin's evenings belonged to his uncle's medical store in Indore until nine. By the time he got home, he was too tired to think about job hunting, and each night he promised to message alumni "tomorrow." Two weeks passed with zero messages. Then he wrote a rule on a sticky note and put it on the counter: "If it's eight and a weekday, two alumni messages go out before I eat." At eight, the store usually went quiet between the office crowd and the late customers. So at eight, between receipts and restocking, he opened his phone and sent two short messages: who he was, his project, a request for ten minutes. On the ninth evening, an alumna, Farida, replied: "Call me Saturday." Sachin grinned at the counter so widely that his uncle asked what was wrong.

qa.q: What time did the store usually go quiet?
How did Sachin feel when Farida replied?
qa.a: Sachin was thrilled, grinning so widely that his uncle asked what was wrong.

qa.q: What else could Sachin add to the rule for busy nights?
qa.a: He could keep a few message drafts ready, so even if the store is busy at eight he can still send two quickly before dinner.

qa.q: How might Farida see Sachin's short message?
qa.a: Farida gets a clear, polite request with his project and a small ask, which makes it easy to agree to a call.

grounding: Illustrates a student with a part-time job using an if-then rule to send two alumni messages at 8 pm on weekdays, removing the daily debate.
